text: The carrier comes out at night, and for a long stretch of the film nobody yet knows what they are looking for. Juan Bautista Stagnaro built his picture around the working life of Salvador Mazza and the colleagues who went into the Argentine interior after an illness that was killing people and had no antidote. It is a drama of procedure: samples, notebooks, argument between professionals, the distance from one house to the next, and at the end of every distance somebody sick. Stagnaro keeps his doctor a worker rather than a man of destiny, the harder way to hold an audience and the reason the pacing matters. Chagas has a name now. The film is interested in the years when it did not, when a case had to be assembled by people travelling a long way to collect very little.

He answers to Third, and the nickname is doing work a name should do. Yōichi Higashi follows a young man with nothing to get up for, drifting alongside two girls who sell themselves part-time and making himself useful to them in the small, ugly way a pimp is useful. The film does not raise its voice about any of it. Drift is the subject rather than a runway toward a lesson, and when trouble arrives, a gangster and a quarrel and a line crossed, it arrives the way an errand does, on an ordinary afternoon, with nothing to announce that a life has changed. Higashi is more curious about how the boy talks than about what he did: the evasions, the flat agreeable tone, the long stretches in which he cannot name one thing he wants. Japan, 1978, and nobody on screen has a plan.

A man turns up at the door and says he is the father who left. Shinji Sōmai drops that claim into the house of a salaryman whose firm is already in trouble, then declines to stage the reckoning the setup promises; the film stays with meals, errands, the ordinary traffic of a household absorbing one more person it did not ask for. Comedy and something bruised keep trading places, sometimes inside a single shot, which is why the tone is hard to describe and easy to recognize. The money trouble is not a subplot. It is the reason a man has no spare capacity for his own past standing in the hallway. Sōmai is patient with the conversation nobody in the house will start, and very funny about the small business people transact instead of starting it.

Seventeen minutes, no narration, and usually more than one thing happening on the screen at once. Christopher Chapman made it for the Ontario Department of Economics and Development, to run at the province's pavilion at Expo '67 in Montreal, built for strangers wandering in at any moment, with nothing to catch up on and a booster song where a voice-over would normally sit. The commission is the interesting part. Chapman splits and recombines the frame so that a province arrives as simultaneity rather than as a tour, and the eye has to choose what to follow. It took the Academy Award for documentary short subject. An economics department paid for a film about how much can be held in view at once, which is not what such a department usually gets for its money.

The crime is dispatched early, almost impatiently, and what remains is custody. Susumu Hani gives his eighty-nine minutes to the interior of a juvenile facility: the pecking order among the boys, the routine, the long unfilled hours in which a young man has nothing to do but account for himself to nobody in particular. The compression tells, since the material never gets room to swell into a statement about youth. What fills the film instead is behavior. How fast a hierarchy forms in a room with nothing in it, how a boy's voice changes when someone official is listening, how ordinary an institution looks from inside it. Hani watches as though watching were sufficient, and for the length of the picture it is. The robbery, by then, has stopped mattering to everyone including the film.

The mission is a pig: one DNA sample from an engineered animal, carried north, to do something about a famine. Lee Chul-jin comes ashore on the eastern coast of the South with that assignment, and Jang Jin plays it straight, an infiltrator with a shopping list, which is funnier than winking would be and, after a while, worse. The joke will not close, because the reason for the errand does not improve on inspection: a state has decided this is what will feed its people, and has sent one man to fetch it. Most of the film lives in the gap between the South an agent was trained to expect and the South he actually walks into. Competence coming apart, with hunger underneath it, made in 1999 about a man who cannot go home empty-handed.

Fifteen years after her husband disappeared in the war, Heeva Akbari decides to go back and look at the house where they lived. The premise is that small. A disappearance is not a death, and the difference is partly a matter of paperwork and entirely consuming; a woman who has lived inside it this long has built a life on a question that was never answered and never withdrawn. Rasoul Mollagholipour lets the house carry the argument. Rooms keep the arrangements people made for a life that then stopped, and walking back into them is a decision whose cost she can predict and takes anyway. It won the Crystal Simorgh for best film, from the country whose war this was, for a story in which the front is never reached and the fighting is fifteen years finished.

In 1909 Sweden stopped working, and in one wealthy Stockholm household the person who did not stop was the maid. Hjördis keeps the house running while the general strike settles over the city, which puts her in a position Vilgot Sjöman is precise about: she sells her labor, she lives inside her employer's home, and the strike is being conducted by people who can withdraw theirs. A hundred and forty-two minutes is long, and the length does something. Domestic service stops reading as backdrop and starts reading as a schedule, hour after hour of it. The politics of the year can only enter this house sideways, as talk, as an interruption to a delivery, as a change in the temperature of a room. The strike is national and offstage; the film is one staircase and the people going up and down it.

Two attacks are named in the title, and the film spends most of its length keeping them waiting. Kajirō Yamamoto gives nearly two hours to cadets: classrooms, drill, instructors, the long apprenticeship of naval airmen before any of them are sent anywhere. It was made in 1942, inside the war it depicts, for a country in the middle of it, which explains where the emphasis falls. Preparation is the pleasure being offered and obedience is the skill on display. Kinema Junpo named it the best Japanese film of the year, a verdict that belongs to the record of 1942 as much as the picture does. What is left now is a document of what a state wanted its people to spend two hours looking at: training grounds, discipline, and the making of willingness in very young men.

The delta is not open country but a scatter of islands with water where roads would be. The family in this film was arranged by that geography long before anything happens to them. Lucas Demare adds one person to it, a girlfriend the son brings home, and the arrangement that the water enforced stops holding. Carancha's jealousy is the engine, and the place is what makes it inevitable rather than merely unpleasant: nobody can walk off to cool down, no evening ends with a guest going home, and four people who all understand the situation keep sharing the same few rooms and the same water. The Silver Condor for best film went to it. Demare applies the pressure slowly, in a setting that supplies its own walls and needs no one to lock a door.

A four-hour serial from 1927 survives as two pieces, and this is one of them. Daisuke Itō was working with a hero his audience already knew by heart: Chuji Kunisada, gambler and outlaw, the property of cheap serialized fiction much as Jesse James was elsewhere. Itō's version has an argument inside the adventure. The class machinery of Edo Japan is treated as something to push against rather than as costume, and the attempt to get the geisha Oshina clear of trouble is the occasion for pushing. There are socialist sympathies in it, plainly. What startles about the surviving reels is the temperature. This is not a careful antique to be handled with gloves; it moves fast, it is angry in places, and the anger is aimed at an arrangement of society rather than at a villain.

She takes a room in a house where the woman who owns it cannot get out of bed and four children have organized things their own way. Leopoldo Torre Nilsson keeps most of the film at that address, and the real subject is how fast a lodger stops being one: the student who came only to lodge starts holding the household together and finds she likes it, or needs it, or cannot tell the two apart. Outside there is a suitor, an attorney with a reasonable offer and a phrase for the house. He calls it a lunatic asylum. He is not entirely wrong, which is the trap. Torre Nilsson makes the sensible life look thin and the strange one look inhabited, then leaves the student standing between them while everyone waits.
